e.abba: Aramaic for “Father,” an affectionate family word. Jesus using it in prayer to God was striking.
e.abomination of desolation: Daniel’s phrase for the temple being desecrated, recalling Antiochus IV setting up a pagan altar there in 167 BC. Jesus warns of a repeat.
e.affliction: Thlipsis literally means pressure, like grapes squeezed in a press, and was used for the hardship expected before the end.
e.tribulation: Thlipsis literally means pressure, like grapes squeezed in a press, and was used for the hardship expected before the end.
e.all authority: Echoes Daniel 7, where a son of man receives all authority from God. Rome claimed that authority for Caesar.
e.almsgiving: Giving to the poor stood beside prayer and fasting as the three pillars of Jewish piety.
e.anguish: Agonia was used for an athlete’s tension before a contest; only Luke records Jesus’ sweat falling like drops of blood.
e.anointed: Kings and priests were anointed with oil. Reading Isaiah 61 in Nazareth, Jesus claims a Spirit anointing.
e.apostles: A sent envoy carried the full authority of the one who sent him. Twelve matched Israel’s twelve tribes.
e.beelzebul: Likely from Baal-zebub, a Philistine god (2 Kings 1); by Jesus’ day a name for the prince of demons.
e.before abraham was born, i am: “I am” echoes God’s name in Exodus 3:14, and the crowd reaches for stones because they hear it as blasphemy.
e.beginning with moses: Jews grouped their Scriptures as the Law (Moses), the Prophets and the Writings, so this means the whole Bible.
e.birth pains: Jewish writers spoke of the “birth pains of the Messiah,” the suffering expected before the new age.
e.blasphemy: Insulting God. The penalty was stoning, which is why the Sanhedrin used the charge against Jesus.
e.blind guides: Teachers saw themselves as guides to the blind (Romans 2:19), so Jesus turns the title upside down.
e.boanerges: A nickname for James and John meaning “sons of thunder,” probably for their fiery temper (Luke 9:54).
e.born again: Greek anothen means both “again” and “from above.” Nicodemus hears the first and Jesus means both.
e.brood of vipers: A desert picture of snakes fleeing a grass fire, used to say that running from judgment won’t save them.
e.charcoal fire: Peter denied Jesus at a charcoal fire in the high priest’s courtyard, and John uses the same rare word for the fire where Jesus cooks breakfast.
e.church: Ekklesia was the citizen assembly of a Greek city, called together by a herald. The Greek Old Testament used it for Israel gathered.
e.clean: “Clean” was ritual status. Skin diseases like those called leprosy meant exclusion until a priest declared you clean (Leviticus 13–14).
e.cleansed: “Clean” was ritual status. Skin diseases like those called leprosy meant exclusion until a priest declared you clean (Leviticus 13–14).
e.cornerstone: Builders set a large foundation stone first and aligned the rest on it. Jesus applies Psalm 118:22 to himself.
e.count the cost: An abandoned half-built tower was a public shame in an honor culture, so counting the cost first was common sense.
e.covenant: A covenant was a binding agreement sealed by sacrifice or a meal. Jeremiah 31 promised a new one, which Jesus announces at the Passover meal.
e.new covenant: A covenant was a binding agreement sealed by sacrifice or a meal. Jeremiah 31 promised a new one, which Jesus announces at the Passover meal.
e.daily: Epiousios barely appears outside the Lord’s Prayer, so whether it means “daily” or “for tomorrow” is debated.
e.daughter of abraham: Calling a woman a “daughter of Abraham” was rare and affirmed her full place in the covenant people.
e.deeply moved: Embrimaomai suggests a snort of indignation, like a horse. John uses it at Lazarus’ tomb.
e.den of robbers: Jeremiah 7 used the phrase of the temple, where people shelter after their crimes. Jesus quotes it while clearing the money changers.
e.house of prayer / den of robbers: Jeremiah 7 used the phrase of the temple, where people shelter after their crimes. Jesus quotes it while clearing the money changers.
e.deny: To disown, as Peter later disowns Jesus. Taking up a cross, a Roman tool of execution, was a vivid picture of giving up your life.
e.deny himself: To disown, as Peter later disowns Jesus. Taking up a cross, a Roman tool of execution, was a vivid picture of giving up your life.
e.departure: Luke uses exodos: Jesus’ “departure” in Jerusalem echoes Israel’s Exodus, a deliverance accomplished through him.
e.distracted: Hosting a teacher and his disciples was a big job in a home-hospitality culture, which explains Martha’s pull.
e.dogs: Jews sometimes used “dogs” as a slur for Gentiles. Jesus’ word is the gentler “little dogs” of the household.
e.dropsy: A swelling disease; the scene is a Sabbath meal at a Pharisee’s house.
e.eli, eli, lema sabachthani: Aramaic from Psalm 22:1. Some bystanders thought he called for Elijah because the sounds are close.
e.eloi, eloi, lema sabachthani: Aramaic from Psalm 22:1. Some bystanders thought he called for Elijah because the sounds are close.
e.elijah: Malachi said Elijah would return before the day of the LORD, so many expected him. Jesus says John the Baptist is that figure.
e.ephphatha: Aramaic for “be opened.” Mark keeps the foreign word as a memory of how Jesus really spoke.
e.eternal life: “Eternal” means belonging to the age to come. Jews expected that age after the resurrection, and John says it starts now.
e.eye of a needle: A proverb for the impossible: the camel was the largest animal people knew.
e.first day of the week: Jews counted days from the Sabbath, so this is Sunday, the day Christians later gathered.
e.fishers of men: Fishing was a major trade around the lake, and Jeremiah 16:16 uses fishing for gathering people. Jesus gives it a new purpose.
e.genealogy: Genealogies proved belonging and inheritance. Matthew includes four women, which was unusual in Jewish family lists.
e.generous: In Hebrew idiom an “evil eye” meant stinginess, so a “good eye” was generosity (Matthew 20:15).
e.glorify: To give weight and honor. In John, Jesus’ glory is paradoxically shown on the cross.
e.good shepherd: Shepherd was a title for kings and for God (Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34), and false shepherds were a prophet’s complaint, so Jesus’ claim is bold.
e.greed: Pleonexia, the desire for more, was condemned by Greek moralists as the root of injustice.
e.grumble: Echoes Israel grumbling in the wilderness over manna, fitting a chapter about bread from heaven.
e.hades: The Greek realm of the dead, like Hebrew sheol, a shadowy waiting place rather than the “hell” of later imagery.
e.hardness of heart: A Hebrew idiom for stubborn refusal to listen, recalling Pharaoh.
e.have mercy: “Have mercy” was the beggar’s cry for help, not only a religious phrase.
e.helper: Parakletos: one called alongside to help, like an advocate in court.
e.hosanna: Hebrew for “save now!” from Psalm 118, shouted by pilgrims at festivals and by crowds greeting a king.
e.humble: In a culture ranked by honor, humility meant low status, so Jesus making it a virtue was a reversal.
e.hypocrisy: A hypocrite was a Greek stage actor wearing a mask, so the word means playing a part.
e.i am he: “I am” echoes God’s own name, which is why the arresting soldiers draw back and fall.
e.i am the bread of life: The crowd had just asked for bread from heaven like Moses’ manna, and Jesus says he is it.
e.i am the light of the world: Said around the Feast of Tabernacles, which included a lamp-lighting ceremony in the temple, so the image would have been vivid.
e.i am the resurrection and the life: Martha believed in resurrection “at the last day.” Jesus makes it a person, present now.
e.i am the way, the truth, and the life: Said to disciples about to lose him. “The Way” later became one of the earliest names for Christians (Acts 9:2).
e.i and the father are one: Said at the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah). The crowd picks up stones because they hear a claim to deity.
e.immanuel: From Isaiah 7:14, “God with us,” a sign to King Ahaz in a political crisis that Matthew applies to Jesus.
e.immediately: Mark’s favorite word (euthys), used dozens of times, gives his Gospel its breathless pace.
e.in remembrance of me: The Passover meal was itself a remembrance of the exodus, and Jesus gives the bread and cup a new one.
e.inn: The road from Jerusalem to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet through desert hills known for robbers.
e.it is finished: Tetelestai was used for completing a task and, on receipts, for a debt paid.
e.it is i: Literally “I am,” echoing God’s name, spoken as Jesus walks on a sea that Job 9:8 says only God treads.
e.jesus wept: The Greek is a quiet weeping, distinct from the loud wailing of the mourners.
e.justified: A courtroom word: declared righteous. The tax collector goes home declared right with God.
e.keep watch: Night was divided into watches, so this means staying awake at your post like servants waiting for their master.
e.lamb of god: Passover lambs, the daily temple lamb and Isaiah 53’s servant “like a lamb” all stand behind this title.
e.leavened: Leaven was a bit of old fermented dough. The woman’s three measures of flour is a large batch, enough for a feast.
e.legion: A Roman legion was several thousand soldiers, so the name draws on the occupying army’s symbol of power.
e.listen to him: Echoes Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promises a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear.
e.living water: Living water meant fresh, flowing spring water, prized over stored cistern water.
e.magi: Magi were Persian-style priest-astronomers who studied the stars. Matthew never says there were three.
e.make disciples: A disciple was an apprentice who learned by living with the teacher; here the call extends to all nations.
e.mercy: Mercy translates Hebrew chesed, faithful covenant love, not merely feeling sorry.
e.minas: A mina was about a hundred denarii, roughly three months’ wages for a laborer.
e.money: Mammon is Aramaic for wealth, almost personified as a rival master.
e.worldly wealth: Mammon is Aramaic for wealth, almost personified as a rival master.
e.mystery: In Daniel a “mystery” is a hidden thing God reveals. The kingdom is hidden to outsiders and revealed to disciples.
e.mysteries: In Daniel a “mystery” is a hidden thing God reveals. The kingdom is hidden to outsiders and revealed to disciples.
e.nazarene: Nazareth was a tiny Galilean village, so “Nazarene” was a tag of obscurity.
e.neighbor: For many Jews “neighbor” meant fellow Israelites. The Samaritan story stretches it to include an enemy.
e.new commandment: The Law already said to love your neighbor; the new part is “as I have loved you.” Latin mandatum gives us “Maundy” Thursday.
e.one flesh: From Genesis 2:24. In a world where a man could easily divorce, Jesus roots marriage in creation.
e.one flock and one shepherd: Ezekiel 34 promised God would gather scattered sheep. Here Jesus includes sheep beyond Israel.
e.orderly: Luke writes in the style of Greek historians who dedicated careful accounts to a patron.
e.overshadow: Used for the cloud covering the tabernacle in Exodus, so God’s presence rests on Mary.
e.paradise: A Persian loan word for a walled royal garden, later used for the place of the blessed.
e.perfect: Teleios means whole or complete rather than flawless; the picture is maturity.
e.persistence: Anaideia means shameless boldness. In a hospitality culture a friend knocking at midnight shames the host into helping.
e.poverty: The widow’s two small copper coins were the smallest in circulation.
e.prunes: Same root as “clean”: vinedressers cleaned and trimmed branches so they would bear more fruit.
e.rabboni: An Aramaic, more personal form of “rabbi”: “my teacher.”
e.ransom: Lytron was the price paid to free a slave or prisoner of war. Jesus says his life is that price.
e.redemption: Used for buying back slaves or prisoners, with Israel’s Exodus as the pattern.
e.render / give back: A denarius carried Caesar’s face and title, so the coin was his; people bear God’s image, so they belong to God.
e.repent: Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
e.repentance: Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
e.repents: Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
e.rock: Simon’s new name, Cephas in Aramaic, means rock.
e.salt: Salt preserved, seasoned and sealed covenants, and it was used in temple sacrifices.
e.sanctify: To set apart for God, as the priests, temple and Sabbath were.
e.savior: Used for gods and for emperors like Augustus. Luke gives the title to a baby in a manger; John has Samaritans say it.
e.savior of the world: Used for gods and for emperors like Augustus. Luke gives the title to a baby in a manger; John has Samaritans say it.
e.sent: John notes that Siloam means “sent,” the pool where the blind man was told to wash.
e.serve: Diakonos meant waiting on tables, a low-status job, which Jesus takes on himself.
e.seventy-seven times: Echoes Lamech’s seventy-sevenfold vengeance in Genesis 4:24, reversed into forgiveness.
e.sift: Wheat was shaken in a sieve to separate grain from chaff, and Satan asks to do that to Peter.
e.son of david: A messianic title; a blind man calling it out shows he sees who Jesus is.
e.son of man: From Daniel 7, a human figure given everlasting rule. In Aramaic it can also just mean “a human being.”
e.stone pavement: Its Aramaic name is Gabbatha, where Pilate sat in judgment; its exact location is debated.
e.stumbling blocks: A skandalon was the trigger of a trap, so to cause stumbling is to set a snare.
e.talitha koum: Aramaic for “little girl, get up.” Mark preserves the Aramaic words Jesus spoke.
e.the abyss: The bottomless deep, which Jewish writing treated as a prison for evil spirits.
e.the hour has come: In John “the hour” is the appointed time of Jesus’ death and glory, which he had said had not yet come.
e.the times of the gentiles: Jerusalem was under Gentile rule, and Luke 21 uses the phrase for the period of Gentile domination.
e.the truth will set you free: Said to listeners who claimed never to have been enslaved, despite Egypt, Babylon and Rome.
e.tradition: The “traditions of the elders” were oral rules layered on the written Law, such as washing hands before meals.
e.transfigured: Metamorphoo gives us “metamorphosis,” and Moses and Elijah, who also met God on mountains, appear with him.
e.treasure: With no banks, people buried valuables in the ground, so finding treasure in a field is believable.
e.veil: A curtain screened the Holy of Holies, which only the high priest entered, once a year on the Day of Atonement.
e.vine: Israel was often pictured as God’s vine or vineyard (Isaiah 5, Psalm 80), and Jesus claims to be the true one.
e.virgin: Isaiah 7:14 in Hebrew says “young woman”; the Greek translation Matthew quotes says parthenos, “virgin.”
e.visitation: Episkope means God coming to inspect or rescue; Luke says Jerusalem missed God’s coming.
e.weeds: Darnel looks like wheat until it heads out, and Roman law had penalties for sowing it in an enemy’s field.
e.weightier matters: Tithing herbs like mint and dill was careful law-keeping, and Jesus says the heavy matters are justice, mercy and faithfulness.
e.well pleased: Combines Psalm 2:7 (the royal son) and Isaiah 42:1 (the servant).
e.whitewashed: Tombs were whitewashed so people could see them and avoid contact and uncleanness.
e.winnowing fork: Farmers tossed grain in the air with a fork so the wind blew the chaff away, a ready picture of judgment.
e.witnesses: Jewish law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter.
e.yoke: A yoke joins two animals to pull a load. Rabbis spoke of the “yoke of the Law” and the “yoke of the kingdom.”
e.zeal: “Zeal for your house” echoes Psalm 69, and “Zealot” later became a name for revolutionaries.
e.gospel: “Good news” was language for royal announcements, like an emperor’s accession or victory.
e.the christ: Greek for “Messiah,” the anointed one, a hoped-for king from David’s line.
e.son of god: “Son of” could mean sharing a character, and Rome styled Caesar Augustus a “son of god.”
e.shepherd: Shepherds were low in status, yet “shepherd” was also a title for kings and for God.
e.my time has not yet come: Kairos means the appointed moment, which John ties to God’s timing rather than the calendar.
e.this generation: A generation was about forty years in biblical thinking; “this generation” can recall the wilderness generation.
e.to the end of the age: Jews spoke of “this age” and “the age to come.”
e.testimony: Jewish law required two or three witnesses, which is why John lines up witnesses for Jesus.
e.testing, temptation: Both “test” and “tempt.” God tests to prove faith, Satan tempts to make it fail, and the wilderness echoes Israel’s forty years.
